title: GP Advice for Anxiety
h1: When Should I Speak To A GP About Anxiety?
description: Learn when to discuss anxiety with a GP, what an appointment involves and what support may be available.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Recognising when anxiety is affecting daily life
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i speak to a gp about anxiety
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Mental Health When Should I Speak To A GP About Anxiety? Learn when anxiety may be worth discussing with a GP, what an appointment may cover and how general practice can connect you with appropriate support. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Anxiety is a normal human response, but it can become difficult when worry, physical symptoms or avoidance start affecting sleep, work, relationships or everyday activities. You do not need to wait until anxiety feels severe before raising it with a GP. Why This Topic Matters Not all worry is an illness. The important questions are whether it continues, feels difficult to control or limits everyday life. Early discussion can identify helpful steps before avoidance, poor sleep or physical distress become established patterns. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Anxiety is not always obvious to the person experiencing it. You might notice repeated reassurance-seeking, reluctance to attend work or social activities, or physical sensations such as trembling or a racing heartbeat. New chest pain or severe breathlessness must not be assumed to be anxiety. Worry is taking time away from normal activities or relationships. Sleep and concentration are repeatedly disrupted. Panic-like episodes are new, distressing or increasing in frequency. Recognising when anxiety is affecting daily life Anxiety can show up as persistent worry, racing thoughts, irritability, difficulty concentrating, sleep problems, muscle tension, a racing heart, breathlessness or avoiding situations that feel overwhelming. What matters is not only the symptom itself, but how often it happens, how intense it feels and whether it is changing what you can comfortably do. A GP can also consider physical conditions, medicines, caffeine, alcohol or other factors that may contribute to similar symptoms. Worry is difficult to control or keeps returning Symptoms are affecting sleep, concentration, study or work You are avoiding activities, appointments, travel or social situations because of anxiety Panic symptoms or physical sensations are causing concern You would like help understanding treatment or referral options When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book medical advice if anxiety is persistent, escalating or interfering with your usual life. If you feel at immediate risk of harming yourself or someone else, or cannot stay safe, call 000 or attend the nearest emergency department. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can listen to what has been happening, review physical and mental health factors, discuss evidence-based treatment options and, when appropriate, prepare a mental health treatment plan or referral. Follow-up is useful because support often works best when progress can be reviewed over time. Patients from Woolloongabba, East Brisbane and nearby inner-south communities can start with a GP when they are unsure what kind of mental health support may be appropriate. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a diagnosis before speaking to a GP? No. You can book because you are worried about how you feel or function. Assessment comes before deciding whether a diagnosis is appropriate. Can anxiety cause physical symptoms? Yes. Anxiety can be associated with symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, stomach discomfort and muscle tension. New or concerning physical symptoms still deserve medical assessment. Can I ask for a longer appointment? Yes. Mental health discussions can take time, so asking reception about a longer appointment may be helpful. title: Anxiety vs Stress
h1: Anxiety vs Stress: What Is The Difference?
description: Understand common differences between stress and anxiety, where they overlap and when a GP review may help.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Stress often has a trigger; anxiety can continue beyond it
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles anxiety vs stress what is the difference
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Mental Health Anxiety vs Stress: What Is The Difference? Understand common differences between stress and anxiety, where they overlap and when a GP review may help. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Stress and anxiety can feel similar. Both may affect sleep, concentration, mood and the body, but they are not always the same experience. Understanding the pattern can help you decide when extra support may be useful. Why This Topic Matters Stress often responds to a recognisable pressure, such as an examination or financial problem. Anxiety may persist when there is no immediate threat. Both can be significant, and the distinction can help determine whether coping strategies, assessment or psychological treatment may be useful. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Common overlaps include poor sleep, irritability, headaches, muscle tension and difficulty concentrating. Notice whether symptoms settle after the pressure passes, whether fears feel out of proportion to events, and whether avoidance is increasing. A stressful event has ended but intense worry continues. Physical symptoms are affecting eating, sleep or daily tasks. You are unsure whether medication, illness or substance use could be contributing. Stress often has a trigger; anxiety can continue beyond it Stress commonly develops in response to demands such as work pressure, study, caregiving, financial problems, illness or major life changes. It may improve when the situation settles or when practical supports are put in place. Anxiety can also be triggered by stressful events, but worry or fear may continue, feel out of proportion to the situation or lead to avoidance. People can experience both stress and an anxiety condition at the same time. Notice whether symptoms ease when the stressful situation changes Pay attention to avoidance, panic or worry that feels hard to control Consider how sleep, alcohol, caffeine and physical health may be contributing Seek support if symptoms are persistent or affecting daily functioning When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Speak with a GP if stress or anxiety is affecting sleep, relationships, work, study or your ability to manage normal tasks. Urgent help is needed if you are at immediate risk of self-harm or cannot keep yourself safe. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can help clarify the pattern, assess for physical contributors, discuss coping strategies and treatment options, and connect you with psychological or other support when appropriate. Patients from Woolloongabba, East Brisbane and nearby inner-south communities can start with a GP when they are unsure what kind of mental health support may be appropriate. Frequently Asked Questions Can stress turn into anxiety? Long-lasting stress can contribute to anxiety symptoms, but there is no single pathway. A GP can help assess what is happening in your situation. Does anxiety always need medicine? No. Treatment is individual and may include psychological strategies, lifestyle measures, medicines or a combination, depending on symptoms and preferences. What should I bring to the appointment? It can help to note when symptoms began, common triggers, sleep changes, medicines and how symptoms are affecting daily life. title: Mental Health Care Plans
h1: What Happens During A Mental Health Care Plan?
description: A practical guide to what a GP mental health assessment and treatment planning appointment may involve in Australia.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
A structured conversation about your health and support needs
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles what happens during a mental health care plan
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Mental Health What Happens During A Mental Health Care Plan? A practical guide to what a GP mental health assessment and treatment planning appointment may involve in Australia. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction A mental health treatment plan is one way a GP can organise care when mental health symptoms need more structured support. The appointment is not simply paperwork: it is an opportunity to understand what you are experiencing and agree on an appropriate care pathway. Why This Topic Matters A mental health treatment plan is a clinical assessment and shared approach to support, not a form automatically provided to everyone. Your GP considers symptoms, functioning, risks, preferences and available therapies before deciding whether a plan is appropriate. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise You may be asked about mood, sleep, anxiety, social support, existing treatment and safety. You can bring notes or request extra time. Medicare eligibility and available subsidised allied mental health sessions depend on current rules and individual circumstances. You would like to discuss psychological therapy options. Symptoms interfere with relationships, employment or study. You need to review an existing treatment plan or ask about follow-up. A structured conversation about your health and support needs Your GP may ask about symptoms, sleep, mood, anxiety, day-to-day functioning, physical health, medicines, alcohol or other substances, relationships, work and safety. Some questions can feel personal, but they help build a fuller picture. If a treatment plan is clinically appropriate, the GP can discuss goals, treatment options, referrals and follow-up. Medicare arrangements and referral eligibility can change, so current entitlements should be confirmed rather than assumed from older information. Allow enough appointment time for a meaningful assessment Bring a medicines list and relevant previous mental health information if available Think about the main changes you want help with Ask what follow-up is recommended and how referrals will work When Should I Seek Medical Advice? You can speak with a GP whenever mental health concerns are persistent, distressing or affecting daily life. You do not need to wait for a crisis. For immediate danger or an inability to stay safe, call 000. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess your current needs, consider whether a mental health treatment plan is appropriate, arrange eligible referrals, discuss medicines when relevant and coordinate ongoing reviews. Patients from Woolloongabba, East Brisbane and nearby inner-south communities can start with a GP when they are unsure what kind of mental health support may be appropriate. Frequently Asked Questions Is a mental health treatment plan automatic if I ask for one? No. Your GP first assesses your needs and whether a plan is clinically appropriate. Will I need to discuss personal information? The GP may ask about symptoms, functioning, safety and other personal factors because these can affect care. You can ask why a question is relevant. How many psychology visits does Medicare cover? Entitlements and referral rules can change. Your GP and Services Australia can confirm current Medicare arrangements for your circumstances. title: How a GP Can Help With Depression
h1: How Can A GP Help With Depression?
description: Learn how a GP can assess low mood and depression, discuss treatment options, coordinate referrals and provide ongoing follow-up.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Depression care is individual and often involves follow-up
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles how can a gp support depression
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Mental Health How Can A GP Help With Depression? Learn how a GP can assess low mood and depression, discuss treatment options, coordinate referrals and provide ongoing follow-up. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Depression can affect mood, motivation, sleep, appetite, concentration, relationships and physical wellbeing. A GP is often a practical first point of contact because they can consider mental health alongside physical health and coordinate care over time. Why This Topic Matters Depression can affect energy, thinking, physical health and relationships. Because low mood can also occur with grief, other medical conditions or medicine effects, a careful assessment is more useful than self-diagnosis. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Signs can include persistent sadness or loss of interest, changes in sleep or appetite, fatigue, slowed thinking, guilt and withdrawal. Some people present mainly with aches, irritability or difficulty working rather than describing sadness. Low mood or loss of interest has continued and affects everyday life. You are withdrawing from people or struggling to care for yourself. You have thoughts of self-harm: seek urgent support; call 000 if in immediate danger. Depression care is individual and often involves follow-up A GP may ask how long symptoms have been present, how they affect daily functioning and whether there are changes in sleep, energy, appetite, concentration or enjoyment. They may also consider medical conditions or medicines that can contribute to similar symptoms. Treatment may include psychological support, lifestyle measures, medicines or a combination. The best approach depends on symptom severity, previous treatment, other health conditions, personal preferences and safety. Persistent low mood or loss of interest deserves assessment Physical symptoms and medical contributors may need review Treatment choices should be discussed rather than assumed Planned follow-up helps assess progress, side effects and changing needs When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP if low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness, sleep changes or reduced functioning persist or concern you. If you have suicidal thoughts with immediate danger, call 000 or attend an emergency department. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess symptoms and safety, discuss a treatment plan, arrange psychological or specialist referral when appropriate, prescribe and monitor medicines where indicated, and provide continuity through follow-up appointments. Patients from Woolloongabba, East Brisbane and nearby inner-south communities can start with a GP when they are unsure what kind of mental health support may be appropriate. Frequently Asked Questions Can depression cause physical symptoms? Yes. Depression can affect sleep, appetite, energy, pain and concentration as well as mood. Do I have to take antidepressants? No single treatment is right for everyone. Your GP can discuss psychological, lifestyle and medicine options based on your circumstances. Why are follow-up appointments important? Follow-up allows symptoms, safety, treatment response and side effects to be reviewed and the plan adjusted when needed. title: Burnout: When to Seek Help
h1: When Should I Seek Help For Burnout?
description: Recognise when prolonged stress and burnout symptoms may benefit from a GP review and what support general practice can provide.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Persistent exhaustion deserves more than pushing through
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i seek help for burnout
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Mental Health When Should I Seek Help For Burnout? Recognise when prolonged stress and burnout symptoms may benefit from a GP review and what support general practice can provide. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction People often use the word burnout to describe prolonged exhaustion, reduced motivation, emotional depletion and feeling unable to recover from ongoing demands. Similar symptoms can also occur with anxiety, depression, sleep problems or physical illness, so a medical review can be useful when the pattern persists. Why This Topic Matters Burnout is usually discussed in relation to prolonged workplace stress, but exhaustion can also overlap with depression, anxiety, sleep disorders and physical illness. Identifying the causes matters more than labelling the experience. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise People may notice emotional exhaustion, detachment from work, declining confidence, disturbed sleep and a reduced sense of effectiveness. Watch for symptoms outside work, such as persistent low mood, significant physical changes or loss of enjoyment. Fatigue remains despite rest or planned time off. Work stress is affecting safety, home relationships or daily functioning. You need assessment before deciding on leave, return-to-work or other changes. Persistent exhaustion deserves more than pushing through Burnout-like symptoms may develop gradually. You may notice poor sleep, irritability, difficulty concentrating, reduced performance, withdrawal from activities, headaches or a sense that normal tasks require much more effort. Because these symptoms overlap with other conditions, self-diagnosis can miss treatable contributors. A GP can help distinguish situational stress from a broader mental or physical health problem. Symptoms continue despite rest or time away from the main stressor Sleep, appetite or concentration have changed significantly You feel persistently low, anxious, detached or overwhelmed Work or home responsibilities are becoming difficult to manage You are relying more on alcohol or other substances to cope When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP appointment if exhaustion or stress-related symptoms are persistent, worsening or affecting your ability to function. Seek emergency help if there is immediate risk of self-harm or you cannot remain safe. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review mental and physical contributors, discuss practical changes, support sleep and mental health care, provide medical documentation when clinically appropriate and arrange referrals or follow-up. Patients from Woolloongabba, East Brisbane and nearby inner-south communities can start with a GP when they are unsure what kind of mental health support may be appropriate. Frequently Asked Questions Is burnout a medical diagnosis? The term is commonly used to describe work- or stress-related exhaustion, but similar symptoms can have several causes. A GP can assess the broader picture. Can a GP check for physical causes of fatigue? Yes. Depending on your history and symptoms, a GP may consider physical health causes and whether examination or tests are appropriate. Should I wait until I need time off work? No. Earlier discussion may help identify support and reduce the chance of symptoms becoming more disruptive. title: ADHD Assessment Pathways
description: Questions about ADHD may begin with difficulties at school, work or home.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · ADHD & Neurodiversity ADHD Assessment Pathways Questions about ADHD may begin with difficulties at school, work or home. Assessment is a process that considers developmental history, functioning and other possible explanations for symptoms. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Questions about ADHD may begin with difficulties at school, work or home. Assessment is a process that considers developmental history, functioning and other possible explanations for symptoms. What Is It? ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition associated with patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity that affect everyday life. Diagnosis is not made from a single online quiz or a short symptom checklist. Australian assessment pathways vary by age, professional scope and service availability. Persistent inattention since childhood Difficulty across several settings Questions about specialist assessment Should I Be Concerned? Talk to a GP if longstanding attention, organisation or impulsivity difficulties affect daily functioning. Similar symptoms can arise from poor sleep, anxiety, depression, trauma or other health conditions, which should be considered during assessment. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? A concern about ADHD is usually not an emergency. If someone is in immediate danger, severely distressed or unable to stay safe, call 000 or seek emergency mental health assistance. How Can a GP Help? A GP can discuss the history, review physical and mental health, explain referral options and support interim strategies. Diagnosis and medicine decisions depend on an appropriately qualified clinician and current Queensland requirements; a GP consultation does not guarantee a diagnosis, prescription or referral acceptance. Specific examples of difficulties at school, home or work and any earlier reports may help clarify referral needs. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can an online ADHD test diagnose me? No. Screening tools can suggest discussing concerns with a clinician but cannot establish a diagnosis. Will I be diagnosed at my first GP visit? Usually not. The first appointment may clarify concerns and referral needs; a comprehensive assessment generally requires more information. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · ADHD & Neurodiversity When Should I Seek ADHD Assessment? Many people experience distraction or restlessness. An assessment may be helpful when these difficulties have been persistent, have a developmental history and are significantly affecting everyday life. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Many people experience distraction or restlessness. An assessment may be helpful when these difficulties have been persistent, have a developmental history and are significantly affecting everyday life. What Is It? ADHD symptoms may look different in children and adults. Examples include difficulties organising tasks, completing work, waiting, controlling impulses or managing competing demands. Sleep problems, anxiety and learning difficulties can overlap with ADHD symptoms. Longstanding organisational difficulties Symptoms affecting school, work or relationships Uncertainty about ADHD versus other conditions Should I Be Concerned? Consider a GP appointment if difficulties affect school, employment, relationships or self-care across more than one setting, particularly where there is evidence they began in childhood. In children, feedback from family and educators may be useful. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Immediate risks to safety, self-harm concerns or severe behavioural crises warrant urgent support; call 000 for immediate danger. Routine ADHD assessment is not a crisis service. How Can a GP Help? A GP can explore symptom history, medical and mental health considerations, and whether assessment through a paediatrician, psychiatrist, psychologist or other appropriately qualified professional is suitable. Referral choice and costs should be discussed. Specific examples of difficulties at school, home or work and any earlier reports may help clarify referral needs. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can adults be assessed for ADHD? Yes. Adult assessment considers current functioning and evidence of symptoms beginning in childhood. Is difficulty concentrating always ADHD? No. Sleep, mood, medicines, stress and health conditions can produce similar difficulties. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: Understanding ADHD Referrals
description: A referral is a practical step towards assessment, not a confirmation that someone has ADHD.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · ADHD & Neurodiversity Understanding ADHD Referrals A referral is a practical step towards assessment, not a confirmation that someone has ADHD. Understanding what information may be required can help you prepare. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A referral is a practical step towards assessment, not a confirmation that someone has ADHD. Understanding what information may be required can help you prepare. What Is It? Specialist pathways differ for children and adults and may involve paediatrics, psychiatry or psychology. Availability, public or private options, costs and the professional permitted to diagnose or prescribe medicines are not identical across services. Preparing assessment history and records Questions about referral costs Co-occurring anxiety, sleep or learning issues Should I Be Concerned? Book a GP appointment if you need to discuss an assessment referral, an existing report or co-occurring sleep and mental health problems. Bringing school reports, previous assessments and details of daily difficulties may be helpful, but missing childhood paperwork should not prevent an initial discussion. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Referral delays can be difficult. If mental health or safety deteriorates, seek timely support separately; call 000 for imminent danger. A routine specialist waiting list should not delay urgent assessment of new symptoms. How Can a GP Help? A GP can help select a suitable pathway, write relevant clinical information, assess other conditions and offer ongoing general healthcare. Specific prescribing and assessment arrangements depend on the clinician and current regulations; no booking guarantees a stimulant prescription. Specific examples of difficulties at school, home or work and any earlier reports may help clarify referral needs. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Does a GP referral guarantee an appointment? No. Specialist services have different acceptance criteria, availability and fees. Confirm these with the provider. Can a psychologist assess ADHD? Some appropriately trained psychologists provide diagnostic assessment, but prescribing rights differ. Ask your GP which pathway fits your needs.
